newsitem.title: USA: Congressional panels urge independent counsel.
newsitem.headline: Congressional panels urge independent counsel.

text.p: Republicans on the House and Senate judiciary committees urged Attorney General Janet Reno Thursday to take action that could lead to an independent counsel to investigate campaign funding abuses.
Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch released a letter sent to Reno signed by all 10 Republicans who control the committee seeking an independent counsel.

A similar letter was being sent by Republicans on the House Judiciary Committee urging an outside prosecutor to delve into the growing allegations of improper campaign funds to Democrats to help President Clinton in the 1996 campaign.
The letters trigger a formal process that the Justice Department must follow that could lead to the naming of an independent counsel.

Hatch said in a statement that Democrats, a minority on his committee and in Congress, would not sign the letter that was sent to Reno that asked her to start the procedure for an independent counsel being named.

Judiciary committee Democrats separately said in their own letter to Reno that was released that if it was determined an independent counsel was warranted, the probe should include the "full scope of fund-raising irregularities" involving Republicans as well as Democrats.

In addition, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott announced that the Senate would begin debate Friday on a nonbinding bill calling for appointment of an independent counsel, with a vote possible next week.

Hatch, a Utah Republican, noted that the committee previously had not joined other calls in Congress for an independent counsel but added "recent developments over the past few weeks, however, have persuaded us that such an appointment is now necessary."
His letter argued that an independent counsel appointed from outside of the administration was needed since a Justice Department probe alone could present a real or apparent conflict of interest.

A task force from her Justice Department that includes 31 FBI agents is currently investigating the fund-raising matter including allegations the Chinese may have funnelled money illegally into U.S. campaigns.

"If the FBI truly is investigating these allegations, as is reported, and this invstigation extends to high level Executive Branch officials, it raises an inherent conflict of interest," said the Hatch letter to Reno.

Hatch suggested several areas of inquiry, including fund-raising activities at the White House and activities involving illegal or improper foreign contributions from people associated with the Lippo Group, an international financial conglomerate based in Indonesia.
A spokesman for House Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican, said committee Republicans were sending a letter to Reno asking her to seek an independent counsel.

Earlier Republicans on their own and several Democrats as well Reno to appoint a special prosecutor to investigate widespread reports of irregularities -- nearly all of them involving improper, illegal or questionable donations to Democrats for the 1996 campaign.
She turned down the requests saying there was no "specific, credible evidence" of a crime that would specifically trigger an independent probe.

Under the independent counsel law, a majority of either Republican or Democratic members of the House or Senate judiciary committees can ask the attorney general to start the process toward naming an independent counsel.
Once Reno gets the request she must submit a report within 30 days on whether a preliminary investigation has or will begin and give her reasons.

If she decides to start a preliminary investigation, Reno has another 90 days to decide if there are "reasonable grounds" to believe there should be a further investigation by an independent counsel. If she concludes there are reasonable grounds, she can apply to a special three-judge federal panel that would appoint an outside counsel.
